CORS

Browsers block cross-origin requests by default — the cors middleware is what lets a frontend on a different origin actually call this API.

A Laravel app rendering its own Blade views never runs into this: the page and the API it calls are the same origin (same scheme, host, and port), so the browser never has anything to block. This project is different by design — a JSON-only API (Week 1) meant to be called from a separate frontend, on a different origin (a different port in dev, a different domain entirely once deployed). Browsers refuse cross-origin requests by default — the Same-Origin Policy — unless the server's response explicitly says otherwise via an Access-Control-Allow-Origin header. This has nothing to do with authentication or a JWT being valid; a request blocked by CORS never even reaches a point where that would matter — the browser refuses to let the calling page read the response at all.

cors, like helmet, is a middleware that sets response headers — in this case, exactly the Access-Control-* headers that tell a browser cross-origin access is allowed:

// Figure 6.15: app.js
app.use(cors());

Called with no options, cors() allows every origin — the same "wide open for now" choice config/socket.js already made for Socket.IO's own CORS setting back in Week 5: there's no deployed frontend origin yet to restrict this to. Once the React frontend module has a real dev/production origin, this is the line that would change to cors({ origin: 'https://your-frontend-origin' }) — the same shape of change either project would make once it exists.
